title: Va'etchanan: and I pleaded (Deuteronomy 3:23–26)
hookLine: Moses begs to enter the land and hears "Let it suffice thee"
tomorrow: Va'etchanan: don't forget what you saw (Deuteronomy 4:9)

lines: FORTY YEARS, AND THE FAR BANK IN SIGHT.
cards: Forty years of work. Every crisis carried. And now, with the far bank of the river in sight, the word comes: you won't cross it.
Someone else will. Moses knew this already; it was decided back at the rock in Numbers. But in his farewell he tells his people something they may not have known: that he went back and asked.
He begged. The new portion takes its name from that begging.

teach.b: It begins, in the old Jewish translation: "And I besought the LORD at that time, saying." The Hebrew first word is va'etchanan, and I pleaded, from the root for grace or favor.
Rashi hears in it a request for a free gift, something not earned.

teach.h: LET ME SEE THE GOOD LAND.
teach.b: And what he asks is simple: "Let me go over, I pray Thee, and see the good land." Just let me see it. The rabbis noticed how hard he asked.
A midrash counts the letters of va'etchanan as numbers, and they add up to five hundred fifteen, so the midrash says Moses prayed five hundred fifteen prayers to enter.

teach.h: RAV LACH: LET IT SUFFICE THEE.
teach.b: Then the answer: "Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto Me of this matter." In Hebrew, rav lach. Literally, much to you, or enough for you.
It's a no. A final one. But it isn't silent, and it isn't the end of the conversation.
In the next breath God tells him to climb to the top of Pisgah and look west, north, south and east, and see the land with his eyes.
And to strengthen Joshua, who will lead them across. Rashi hears more than a refusal in rav lach: much good, he says, is already stored up for you.
The portion is read on the Sabbath right after Tisha B'Av, called the Sabbath of comfort. The comfort starts with a man who heard no, and still climbed the mountain to look.

how: Va'etchanan is read in synagogues on the Sabbath after Tisha B'Av, known as Shabbat Nachamu, the Sabbath of comfort, named for the prophetic reading from Isaiah that follows it.

o: and I commanded: Moses giving orders
and I pleaded: Moses asking for grace
and I wept: Moses mourning his brother

games.q: inside the pleading — tap the pairs.
p: the midrash's count of his prayers
where Moses looks at the land

s: Moses never asked to enter the land
"And I besought the LORD at that time": he pleaded to cross.
after the no, God lets Moses see the land from a mountain
from the top of Pisgah, west, north, south and east.
va'etchanan comes from the root for grace or favor
it's asking for a gift, not demanding a right.

games.q: you're Moses. you've asked to cross the Jordan and heard: let it suffice thee; speak no more of this. what do you do?
o: climb the mountain, look, and strengthen Joshua.
games.why: he goes up Pisgah to see the land, and is told to charge and strengthen Joshua, who will lead them across.

practice: Think of a no you've been given lately: a job, an answer, a body that won't do what it used to. Feel how much you wanted it, then say softly, rav lach, enough for you.
Look around the way Moses looked out from the mountain, and name three things you can see from where you stand.

wordCard.voice: Va'etchanan. And I pleaded. Moses' first word in this portion, asking for grace he knows he can't demand.

orig.note: Hebrew: and I pleaded, from the root for grace or favor. its letters add up to 515.

carryVoice: Your line: let it suffice thee. A no can still come with a view. Day four hundred eighty-seven.
